articles.title: Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers might save lives during natural disasters
articles.summary:

The post Indonesia’s mosque loudspeakers might save lives during natural disasters first appeared on The Optimist Daily: Making Solutions the News.
articles.content:
BY THE OPTIMIST DAILY EDITORIAL TEAM

The hardest part of any early warning system isn’t the science. It’s finding infrastructure that reaches everyone, holds up under pressure, and gets maintained over years by the people who depend on it. In Indonesia, a team of Japanese and Indonesian researchers think that infrastructure already exists. It broadcasts the call to prayer five times a day.

With the largest Muslim population in the world, Indonesia has hundreds of thousands of mosques, nearly all equipped with loudspeakers that reach the surrounding community. A five-year pilot project running until 2030 is testing whether those speakers can double as earthquake alert klaxons, connected to a seismic sensor network that sounds an alarm before the shaking arrives. Several mosques have already been hooked up.

The project was conceived by Dr. Inoue Hiroshi of the Disaster Prevention Research Institute at Kyoto University, who came up with the idea while researching deadly earthquakes in Sumatra nearly two decades ago. “Every community has a mosque,” he told the Guardian. The rest of his argument was practical: “The advantage of a mosque speaker is that they’re existing and well maintained. For any disaster infrastructure, maintenance is the big challenge… but the mosque speaker is maintained by the people.”

Mobile phones are the default tool for modern disaster alerts, but phone networks can fail in an earthquake. Mosque loudspeakers, tested five times a day by the communities that run them, are harder to knock out.

The seconds that matter in an earthquake

Earthquake early warning is different from tsunami warning. Tsunamis build over time and can be tracked; communities might have minutes or hours to act. Earthquake waves move through the ground at extraordinary speed. A village 31 miles (50 kilometers) from the epicenter might have only five to ten seconds, according to Andi Eka Sakya, senior researcher at Indonesia’s National Research and Innovation Agency and Indonesian co-lead on the project. The system isn’t issuing public warnings yet, but that’s what the team is working toward.

Dr. Inoue’s interest goes back to a 2009 earthquake in western Sumatra that killed at least 1,000 people. “I thought if Indonesia had the same service and people received the warning before the shaking came, then many people among those few hundred wouldn’t have died,” he says.

Drop and cover doesn’t always apply

What to do with five to ten seconds turns out to be its own research problem. In Japan, official guidelines center on drop and cover: get under a table, stay indoors, ride it out. That advice was written for well-constructed buildings.

In Indonesia and many developing countries, homes are frequently built from unreinforced masonry, which collapses under earthquake stress. In some documented cases in Indonesia, two-story buildings have had the first floor crushed while the second floor stayed relatively intact. The people who survived ran outside. “The way people react is they quickly escape out of the room,” Inoue says. “They know how to survive.”

Standard international guidelines don’t account for that. Project researchers are running simulations and human experiments to develop guidance grounded in how Indonesian buildings actually fail. Survival advice calibrated for the wrong type of building can kill people.

Other countries are exploring the same approach

Uzbekistan’s Ministry of Emergency Situations announced a pilot program this year to install alarm devices in 272 mosques, warning communities about floods, mudflows, landslides, and avalanches. The United Nations Development Programme, which partnered in the initiative, put it plainly: mosques “are traditionally perceived as authoritative social institutions with significant influence on local communities.” A broadcast from a trusted institution reaches people differently than one from a government system most residents have never interacted with.

The Indonesia project is also adding school loudspeakers, radio, and television as backup layers. But the mosque network is the foundation. It was already there, maintained every day by the communities that need it most.

articles.personality_title_fr: Loudspeakers des mosquées en Indonésie pour alerter des tremblements de terre
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’Indonésie est un pays sujet aux tremblements de terre et compte la plus grande population musulmane au monde. La plupart des communautés ont des mosquées équipées de haut-parleurs qui appellent à la prière cinq fois par jour.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Des chercheurs japonais et indonésiens ont lancé un projet pour utiliser ces haut-parleurs comme alarmes sismiques. Ils sont reliés à des capteurs qui détectent les tremblements de terre et peuvent prévenir les habitants quelques secondes avant le début des secousses. Le projet a commencé récemment et durera jusqu’en 2030.

**Impact** – Utiliser les haut-parleurs des mosquées est une bonne idée car ils existent déjà, sont bien entretenus et atteignent beaucoup de personnes autour. Les alertes par téléphone peuvent échouer lors d’un séisme, mais les haut-parleurs des mosquées sont testés chaque jour et sont plus fiables. Cela pourrait sauver de nombreuses vies en donnant quelques secondes pour se préparer.

**Prochaine étape** – L’équipe travaille à donner des conseils adaptés aux maisons indonésiennes, souvent fragiles, car les gens survivent souvent en sortant rapidement. Ils ajoutent aussi des alertes via les écoles, la radio et la télévision pour compléter le système des mosquées.

**Résumé en une phrase** – L’Indonésie transforme les haut-parleurs des mosquées en alarmes sismiques pour avertir rapidement les communautés et aider à sauver des vies grâce à une technologie existante et fiable.

articles.title: Colombia: UN independent experts call for Ecopetrol to provide reparations to victims of armed conflict
articles.summary: UN independent experts welcomed on Wednesday a recent landmark corporate accountability ruling involving the Ecopetrol oil company by Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace, calling for reparations for victims.
articles.content:
The Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) ruling related to the Macro-Case 08, which recognises the responsibility of several State agents and a director of the State-owned company for their involvement in acts related to serious human rights violations, war crimes and crimes against humanity committed during the armed conflict in Barrancabermeja, Colombia’s oil capital.

“The JEP’s decision represents a significant step forward for truth, justice and accountability regarding the impacts of corporate activities in conflict-affected contexts,” the experts said. “It also opens an unprecedented opportunity to place victims at the centre of reparation and restoration efforts.”

The experts welcomed the cooperation provided by Ecopetrol during the proceedings and encouraged the company to deepen that commitment through ongoing dialogue and concrete actions for reparation and restoration aimed at the affected individuals and communities.

Companies must respect human rights

“Companies have a responsibility to respect human rights and to participate in redressing the negative impacts they have caused or contributed to, in accordance with the United Nations Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights,” they noted.

Tweet URL

The experts urged Ecopetrol to continue engaging in good faith in a constructive dialogue with the victims and their representative organisations, adopting a restorative approach that allows for the identification of the harms suffered, expectations for reparations and the measures necessary to help restore the rights violated.

“Victims should not be mere observers of the reparation processes, they must be active participants in their design and implementation,” they said. “Effective reparations require meaningful participation, acknowledgment of harm and a sustained commitment to restoring rights and rebuilding trust.”

State’s duty to protect

As the majority shareholder of Ecopetrol, the experts highlighted the role of the Colombian State in this process.

“When it comes to State-owned enterprises, business responsibilities to respect human rights converge with the State’s duty to protect such rights,” they said.

“Colombian authorities must ensure the company participates fully in efforts towards truth, justice, reparations and guarantees of non-repetition and that this process effectively contributes to strengthening public trust in institutions,” the experts said.

The independent experts, who are appointed by the Human Rights Council, are not UN staff and do not receive a salary, reiterated the call by the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights for sufficient funding of Colombia’s comprehensive peace system, which includes the JEP and the Unit for the Search for Missing Persons.

“We stand ready and willing to support the Government of Colombia and Ecopetrol in this process, in order to strengthen corporate accountability in contexts of transitional justice and to build sustainable peace,” they concluded.
articles.source: UN News - Global perspective Human stories
articles.reasoning: The article reports a landmark ruling holding a major state-owned company accountable for human rights violations during armed conflict, emphasizing reparations and victim participation. This represents significant progress in corporate accountability, transitional justice, and peacebuilding with broad societal impact in Colombia.
articles.personality_title: Colombia’s Ecopetrol urged to provide reparations for conflict victims after historic ruling
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Colombia has faced a long armed conflict that affected many people, including in Barrancabermeja, the country’s oil capital. Ecopetrol, a major state-owned oil company, was involved in actions linked to serious human rights violations during this conflict.

**What happened** – Colombia’s Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP) made a landmark ruling called Macro-Case 08. It found that Ecopetrol and some state agents were responsible for crimes like war crimes and crimes against humanity during the conflict. The ruling calls for Ecopetrol to provide reparations to the victims and involve them in the process.

**Impact** – This is the first time a big company like Ecopetrol has been held accountable in this way in Colombia. The decision focuses on justice and repairing the harm done, not just punishing wrongdoing. It also encourages the company to work closely with victims to understand their needs and help restore their rights.

**What’s next step** – Ecopetrol is expected to continue cooperating and to engage in open dialogue with victims and their representatives. The Colombian government, as the main owner of Ecopetrol, must ensure the company fully takes part in reparations and efforts to prevent future abuses.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Colombia’s peace court has set a new example by requiring Ecopetrol to repair harm to conflict victims, involving them directly in the process to rebuild trust and justice.
articles.personality_title_fr: Colombie : Ecopetrol appelée à réparer les victimes du conflit après une décision historique
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – La Colombie a connu un long conflit armé qui a touché de nombreuses personnes, notamment à Barrancabermeja, capitale pétrolière du pays. Ecopetrol, une grande entreprise pétrolière publique, a été impliquée dans des violations graves des droits humains durant ce conflit.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – La Juridiction spéciale pour la paix (JEP) de Colombie a rendu une décision historique appelée Macro-Procès 08. Elle a reconnu la responsabilité d’Ecopetrol et de certains agents de l’État pour des crimes de guerre et crimes contre l’humanité. La décision demande à Ecopetrol d’indemniser les victimes et de les inclure dans ce processus.

**Impact** – C’est la première fois qu’une grande entreprise comme Ecopetrol est tenue responsable de cette manière en Colombie. Cette décision met l’accent sur la justice et la réparation des torts, au-delà de la punition. Elle encourage aussi l’entreprise à travailler étroitement avec les victimes pour comprendre leurs besoins et restaurer leurs droits.

**Prochaine étape** – Ecopetrol doit continuer à coopérer et dialoguer avec les victimes et leurs représentants. Le gouvernement colombien, principal actionnaire d’Ecopetrol, doit veiller à ce que l’entreprise participe pleinement aux réparations et aux mesures pour éviter de futurs abus.

**Conclusion en une phrase** – Le tribunal de paix colombien donne un nouvel exemple en exigeant qu’Ecopetrol répare les préjudices subis par les victimes du conflit, en les impliquant directement pour reconstruire la confiance et la justice.

articles.title: Social media, kids, and AI: interview with European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen
articles.summary: On Friday, October 9, journalists part of the European Newsroom spoke to Virkkunen about the rapid development of artificial intelligence, as well as the EU’s progress in protecting children online.
articles.content:
On Friday, October 9, journalists part of the European Newsroom spoke to Virkkunen about the rapid development of artificial intelligence, as well as the EU’s progress in protecting children online.

Is artificial intelligence growing more rapidly than humanity’s ability to contain it? The EU’s tech chief had a stark warning for the development of AI systems: if we don’t put guardrails in place now, the technology might soon be beyond our control.

In an interview with the European Newsroom (enr), European Commission Executive Vice-President Henna Virkkunen (Tech Sovereignty, Security and Democracy) said AI systems are becoming more capable and harder to evaluate.

The Finnish politician called for the establishment of international rules, which she said were already being discussed among G7 and G20 countries. She told journalists she was convinced that countries which are currently unwilling to regulate the sector will eventually come around.

China and the United States are currently leading in AI development but are showing no signs of slowing down despite recent warnings from industry insiders. Meanwhile, the EU has already begun to enforce its landmark AI Act.

Virkkunen also spoke about the addictive nature of social media networks and the impact they have on European children, calling on platforms to take greater responsibility. The Commission last month proposed a new law that seeks to limit the use of social media, including restrictions on gaming, for kids under 15.

The interview was conducted by enr news agencies dpa (Germany) and PAP (Poland) on behalf of the enr network.

articles.reasoning: The article highlights the EU's proactive regulatory efforts to protect children online and manage AI development responsibly, which has broad societal significance and positive real-world impact on digital safety and governance.
articles.personality_title: EU pushes new rules to keep kids safe online and control AI growth
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Artificial intelligence (AI) is developing quickly, and social media can sometimes be addictive, especially for children. The European Union (EU) is working to manage these challenges and protect young people online.

**What happened** – On October 9, Henna Virkkunen, a top EU official in charge of technology and security, spoke to journalists about the rapid rise of AI and the EU’s efforts to protect children from harmful online content. She warned that without clear rules, AI could become hard to control. The EU is already enforcing new laws called the AI Act to regulate AI technology. Virkkunen also discussed a recent EU proposal to limit social media use and online gaming for kids under 15.

**Impact** – This is important because it shows the EU is taking early steps to keep technology safe for everyone, especially children. By setting rules for AI and social media, the EU hopes to prevent problems like addiction and misuse of AI before they get worse. The move also encourages other countries to join in making responsible technology rules.

**What's next step** – The EU will continue working with other big countries like the US and China to create international AI rules. The new social media limits for kids will also be discussed and possibly become law soon, helping to protect young users across Europe.

**One-sentence takeaway** – The EU is leading efforts to create smart rules that protect children online and keep artificial intelligence safe and under control.
articles.personality_title_fr: L’UE propose de nouvelles règles pour protéger les enfants en ligne et contrôler l’essor de l’IA
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – L’intelligence artificielle (IA) évolue rapidement, et les réseaux sociaux peuvent être parfois addictifs, surtout pour les enfants. L’Union européenne (UE) travaille à gérer ces défis et à protéger les jeunes en ligne.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Le 9 octobre, Henna Virkkunen, une haute responsable de l’UE chargée de la technologie et de la sécurité, a parlé aux journalistes de la montée rapide de l’IA et des efforts de l’UE pour protéger les enfants contre les contenus en ligne nocifs. Elle a averti que sans règles claires, l’IA pourrait devenir difficile à contrôler. L’UE applique déjà une nouvelle loi appelée l’AI Act pour réguler la technologie IA. Virkkunen a aussi évoqué une proposition récente de l’UE pour limiter l’usage des réseaux sociaux et des jeux en ligne pour les moins de 15 ans.

**Impact** – Cela montre que l’UE prend des mesures précoces pour rendre la technologie sûre pour tous, surtout pour les enfants. En établissant des règles pour l’IA et les réseaux sociaux, l’UE espère prévenir des problèmes comme l’addiction et les mauvais usages de l’IA avant qu’ils ne s’aggravent. Cette démarche encourage aussi d’autres pays à adopter des règles responsables.

**Étape suivante** – L’UE continuera à travailler avec d’autres grandes puissances comme les États-Unis et la Chine pour créer des règles internationales sur l’IA. Les nouvelles limites sur les réseaux sociaux pour les enfants seront aussi discutées et pourraient devenir loi bientôt, aidant à protéger les jeunes utilisateurs partout en Europe.

**Phrase clé** – L’UE mène des efforts pour créer des règles intelligentes qui protègent les enfants en ligne et gardent l’intelligence artificielle sûre et maîtrisée.
articles.personality_title_es: La UE impulsa nuevas reglas para proteger a los niños en línea y controlar el crecimiento de la IA
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – La inteligencia artificial (IA) está creciendo rápidamente, y las redes sociales a veces pueden ser adictivas, especialmente para los niños. La Unión Europea (UE) está trabajando para manejar estos retos y proteger a los jóvenes en internet.

**Qué pasó** – El 9 de octubre, Henna Virkkunen, una alta funcionaria de la UE encargada de tecnología y seguridad, habló con periodistas sobre el rápido avance de la IA y los esfuerzos de la UE para proteger a los niños de contenido dañino en línea. Advirtió que sin reglas claras, la IA podría volverse difícil de controlar. La UE ya está aplicando una nueva ley llamada Ley de IA para regular esta tecnología. Virkkunen también habló sobre una propuesta reciente de la UE para limitar el uso de redes sociales y juegos en línea para niños menores de 15 años.

**Impacto** – Esto es importante porque muestra que la UE está tomando medidas tempranas para mantener la tecnología segura para todos, especialmente para los niños. Al crear reglas para la IA y las redes sociales, la UE quiere evitar problemas como la adicción y el mal uso de la IA antes de que empeoren. Esta iniciativa también anima a otros países a unirse para crear reglas responsables.

**Próximo paso** – La UE seguirá trabajando con otros países grandes como Estados Unidos y China para crear reglas internacionales sobre IA. También se discutirán los nuevos límites para el uso de redes sociales en niños, que podrían convertirse en ley pronto, protegiendo a los jóvenes usuarios en toda Europa.

**Frase clave** – La UE lidera esfuerzos para crear reglas que protejan a los niños en línea y mantengan la inteligencia artificial segura y bajo control.
